According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in ancient times the shrine was built facing west towards the [[Harima Sea]], but because boatmen passing by at sea did not worship there, it caused frequent curses, so it was changed to its current south-southwest orientation.]]{{complex}} '''[[Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji|Yamato Okunitama Shrine]]''' is [[Shinto shrine|a shrine]] located in Enamikamihata, {{ill|Minamiawaji|en|4=fr|lt=Minami Awaji City|12=draft}}, [[Hyogo Prefecture]]. It is a shrine listed in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] as a [[Myojin Taisha]] and is [[Ichinomiya|ninomiya]] or second ranked shrine in [[Awaji Province]], and [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|its former rank]] was [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|that of a prefectural shrine]]..{{Cite web|title=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|url=http://kuniumi-awaji.jp/|access-date=2024-04-07|website=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|language=en}} It is connected to the [[Yamato no Kuni no Miyatsuko|Yamato no Kuni no MIyatsuko]]. == deity == * Main deity: [[Yamato Okunitama|Yamato-Okunitama-no-kami]] * Associated deities: [[Ōkuninushi|Yasengai-no-Mikoto]], [[Toshigami|Oninoshi-no-Mikoto]], [[Susanoo|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]], [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]], [[Landlord deity|Earth God]] According to "A Fundamental Study on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Countries," the deities enshrined in the "Ippen Shonin E" and the Noh play "Awaji" are cited as [[Izanagi|Izanagi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Izanami|Izanami-no-Mikoto]], indicating that in the medieval period, the two deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 The book suggests that such an error occurred because Awaji is the land associated with the creation myth involving Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto, leading to this association by shrine families, as speculated in the "Shikinai-sha Report." It also states that the enshrinement returned to Yamato Okuninushi-no-Kami after the separation of Shinto and Buddhism in the Meiji period. The "Chuko Shujishi," dated August 1670 (Kanbun 10), was also written based on the theory that the deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.『中興趣意書』は、神道大系編纂会編 『神道大系 神社編41 紀伊・淡路国』 神道大系編纂会 1987th year 9月 に所収されている。 == history == The exact date of construction of this shrine is unknown. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, when the power of {{ill|Yamato kingship|lt=the Yamato Imperial Court|en|12=draft}} extended to Awaji, this shrine is believed to have {{ill|Bunrei|lt=enshrined|En|12=draft}} Yamato-no-Okunitama-jinja Shrine (present-day [[Ōyamato Shrine|Yamato Shrine]] ) in {{ill|Yamabe District, Nara|lt=Yamabe District|en|12=draft}}, [[Yamato Province]], in prayer for the stability of its rule. The book "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in the Medieval Provinces" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 introduces the theory that the shrine was established in the 5th century, in connection with the rule of the Yamato court. According to the entry for December 5th, 851 in the " {{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|en}} ," this shrine was designated an official shrine by imperial decree. Furthermore, the entry for January 27, 859 in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|12=draft}} records that the shrine's {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|en|12=draft}} was promoted from Junior Second Rank and Third Class to Junior First Rank . In the year 927 (Engi 5), according to the "Engishiki Jinmyocho," it was designated as a Shikinaisha, and a [[Myojin Taisha]]. Additionally, in the "Sozei" section of the "Engishiki," it received 800 bundles of festival rations (equivalent to 16 koku of rice) from the state. According to the "Engishiki," at that time, only three other shrines besides [[Dewa Province]]'s [[Gassan Shrine]], [[Mutsu Province]]'s [[Shiogama Jinja|Shiogama Shrine]], and [[Izu Province]]'s {{ill|Mishima-taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|12=draft}} were receiving festival rations directly from the state's regular taxes, indicating that this shrine received special treatment from the state. This shrine is known as the second shrine of Awaji Province, but according to "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Various Provinces in the [[Eiman|Middle]] Ages" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。, the first mention of this was in the "Order for Annual Taxes from the Shrines of Various Shrines" 平安遺文3358号 『神祇官諸社年貢注文』は 竹内理三 編 『平安遺文 古文書編 第7巻』 株式会社東京堂出版 1963rd year 10月 に所収されている。 dated [[1165|June 1165]] (the first year of the Eiman era), which stated, "The second shrine of Awaji Province (50 baskets of charcoal and 100 bundles of firewood)." The book also cites the Gokokuji documents 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, including [[Genkyū|the Awaji]] Kokushicho Sensho '''庁宣'''は、現地に赴任しなかった[[国司]]が、[[国衙]]の在庁官人にあてた命令のこと。 dated April [[1205|1205 (the 2nd year of the Genkyu era]] ), which states, “It was ordered to quickly gather information about the First and Second Palace Hokke and Sakura festivals, as well as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields and wilderness areas.” This suggests that the {{ill|10=ja|11=国衙|provincial government|12=draft}} was in charge of the festivals of this shrine, as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields were allocated by the provincial government for the holding of both the Hokke and Sakura festivals. The stone monument in front of the shrine explains how the festival became known to the public as the "Ninomiya Cherry Blossom Festival" because local people would worship the gods and admire the cherry blossoms. Later, the shrine came to be revered as the Ninomiya of Awaji Province, and both the imperial court and the military government became deeply revered. In the past, this Sakura-e festival was held on March 10th, but according to "The Gods of Japan - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, it was discontinued at some point. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" [1 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in [[Shōō (Kamakura period)|July]] [[1289]], the monk {{ill|Ippen|en}} Shonin visited the shrine, composed a poem, wrote it on a wooden tablet, and nailed it to the front of the main shrine building. It is said that this wooden tablet was still there when {{ill|Shōkai|fr|12=draft}}, the editor of "Ippen Hijiri-e," visited the temple after Ippen's death. The book also says that when Ippen Shonin heard that the shrine's deity was Izanami-no-Mikoto, he offered fervent prayers, and even built a hut in front of the shrine, performed dancing {{ill|nembutsu|en}}, and handed out pieces of paper with the words "Namu Amida Butsu" written on them. According to the "Awaji Province Temple and Mountain Memorial Services Order," one of the "Gokokuji Documents" 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, bugaku (traditional dance) performances were offered to the shrine by musicians from Kashu Hachiman (Kashu Hachiman, Minamiawaji City). According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, this took place during [[Muromachi period|the Muromachi period]] . During [[Edo period|the Edo period]], Awaji Province became a fief of the Tokushima Domain, and the {{ill|Hachisuka clan|en|12=draft}} also had deep faith in this shrine, donating two tan of land to the shrine in [[1702]] ( [[Genroku]] 15). Since then, it has been revered as a place of prayer for generations, and the shrine buildings have been renovated many times. In addition to rebuilding the main hall, other [[Bunsei|constructions]], such as the construction of [[Tenpō|other]] halls in [[1829]] and [[1843]], were carried out until the {{ill|abolition of the han system|en|4=fr|5=Abolition du système han|12=draft}} and the establishment of prefectures following [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]] . Due to {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|lt=the Shinto-Buddhist separation order|en|12=draft}} in [[1868]], the Kannon Hall of Yamato-ji Temple, the 12th temple on the Awaji Saigoku Pilgrimage, and the Yakushi Hall, the 2nd temple on the Awaji Forty-nine Yakushi Temples, which were located within the shrine grounds, were moved outside. In [[1873]], under the old shrine ranking system, it was ranked as [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], and [[1877|in 1877]], the main hall and other buildings were all newly built using county funds from believers throughout {{ill|Mihara District, Hyōgo|lt=Mihara County|en|12=draft}}. When the {{ill|10=ja|11=阪神・淡路大震災|Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake|12=draft}} occurred on January 17, [[1995]], the torii gate, which had been erected approximately 400 years ago, was damaged beyond repair, so in December [[1998|1998,]] parishioners from the five districts of Somori, Kamihata, Shimohata, Matsuda, and Yamadokoro worked together to erect the current torii gate. == Festivals == * February 11th: [[National Foundation Day (Japan|National Foundation Day]] * February 17th [[Kinensai|Prayer Festival]] * April 1st {{ill|Reisai|fr|lt=Annual Festival|12=draft}} * July 18th Summer Festival * November 12th [[Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niiname-sai Festival]] == Cultural Assets == === Hyogo Prefecture designated cultural property === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Yamato Company Seal **: According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, the seal is an old bronze seal that was excavated from the temple grounds during [[Hōei|the Hoei era]], measuring 5.5 cm square and engraved with the words "Yamato Shrine Seal." According to the book, it is said to date back to the early Heian period. == footnote == == References == * Edited by Takeuchi Rizo, Heian Ibun Komonsho Volume 7, Tokyodo Publishing Co., Ltd., October 1963 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Series Editing Committee, " National History Series Volume 3: [[Nihon kōki|Nihon Koki]], Shoku Nihon Koki, Nihon Montoku Tenno Jitsuroku " Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., August 1966 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Editing Committee, ed., National History Series, Volume 4 : The Chronicles of the Three Generations of Japan, Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., April 1966 * Edited by the Hyogo Prefecture History Editing Committee, "Hyogo Prefecture History: Historical Materials, Middle Ages 1," Hyogo Prefecture, November 1983 * Kenichi Tanigawa (ed.), "Japanese Gods -Shrines and Sacred Places- 3: Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" Hakusuisha Publishing Co., Ltd., August 1984 * Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee (ed.) Shinto Taikei Shrines Vol. 41 Kii and Awaji Province Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee September 1987 * "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces" edited by the Study Group on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces, Iwata Shoin Co., Ltd., February 2000 {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{afc comment|1=see [[every:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] for the history[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 02:26, 31 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Hyōgo Prefecture]] [[Category:Coordinates on Wikidata]] [[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[Category:Fuken-sha]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:Simple english wikipedia and everybodywiki]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:pages which might possibly be incomplete but are most likely complete]] [[Category:I think I cleared all the incomplete or blank pages earlier]] }} [[en:draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[fr:Yamato_Okunitama-jinja,_Minamiawaji]] [[en:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[sn:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[en:Draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[ja:大和大国魂神社]] [[fr:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama-jinja]]

According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, this took place during [[Muromachi period|the Muromachi period]] . During [[Edo period|the Edo period]], Awaji Province became a fief of the Tokushima Domain, and the {{ill|Hachisuka clan|en|12=draft}} also had deep faith in this shrine, donating two tan of land to the shrine in [[1702]] ( [[Genroku]] 15). Since then, it has been revered as a place of prayer for generations, and the shrine buildings have been renovated many times. In addition to rebuilding the main hall, other [[Bunsei|constructions]], such as the construction of [[Tenpō|other]] halls in [[1829]] and [[1843]], were carried out until the {{ill|abolition of the han system|en|4=fr|5=Abolition du système han|12=draft}} and the establishment of prefectures following [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]] . Due to {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|lt=the Shinto-Buddhist separation order|en|12=draft}} in [[1868]], the Kannon Hall of Yamato-ji Temple, the 12th temple on the Awaji Saigoku Pilgrimage, and the Yakushi Hall, the 2nd temple on the Awaji Forty-nine Yakushi Temples, which were located within the shrine grounds, were moved outside. In [[1873]], under the old shrine ranking system, it was ranked as [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], and [[1877|in 1877]], the main hall and other buildings were all newly built using county funds from believers throughout {{ill|Mihara District, Hyōgo|lt=Mihara County|en|12=draft}}. When the {{ill|10=ja|11=阪神・淡路大震災|Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake|12=draft}} occurred on January 17, [[1995]], the torii gate, which had been erected approximately 400 years ago, was damaged beyond repair, so in December [[1998|1998,]] parishioners from the five districts of Somori, Kamihata, Shimohata, Matsuda, and Yamadokoro worked together to erect the current torii gate. == Festivals == * February 11th: [[National Foundation Day (Japan|National Foundation Day]] * February 17th [[Kinensai|Prayer Festival]] * April 1st {{ill|Reisai|fr|lt=Annual Festival|12=draft}} * July 18th Summer Festival * November 12th [[Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niiname-sai Festival]] == Cultural Assets == === Hyogo Prefecture designated cultural property === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Yamato Company Seal **: According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, the seal is an old bronze seal that was excavated from the temple grounds during [[Hōei|the Hoei era]], measuring 5.5 cm square and engraved with the words "Yamato Shrine Seal." According to the book, it is said to date back to the early Heian period. == footnote == == References == * Edited by Takeuchi Rizo, Heian Ibun Komonsho Volume 7, Tokyodo Publishing Co., Ltd., October 1963 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Series Editing Committee, " National History Series Volume 3: [[Nihon kōki|Nihon Koki]], Shoku Nihon Koki, Nihon Montoku Tenno Jitsuroku " Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., August 1966 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Editing Committee, ed., National History Series, Volume 4 : The Chronicles of the Three Generations of Japan, Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., April 1966 * Edited by the Hyogo Prefecture History Editing Committee, "Hyogo Prefecture History: Historical Materials, Middle Ages 1," Hyogo Prefecture, November 1983 * Kenichi Tanigawa (ed.), "Japanese Gods -Shrines and Sacred Places- 3: Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" Hakusuisha Publishing Co., Ltd., August 1984 * Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee (ed.) Shinto Taikei Shrines Vol. 41 Kii and Awaji Province Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee September 1987 * "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces" edited by the Study Group on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces, Iwata Shoin Co., Ltd., February 2000 {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{afc comment|1=see [[every:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] for the history[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 02:26, 31 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Hyōgo Prefecture]] [[Category:Coordinates on Wikidata]] [[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[Category:Fuken-sha]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:Simple english wikipedia and everybodywiki]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:pages which might possibly be incomplete but are most likely complete]] }} [[en:draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[fr:Yamato_Okunitama-jinja,_Minamiawaji]] [[en:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[sn:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[en:Draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[ja:大和大国魂神社]] [[fr:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama-jinja]]

According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in ancient times the shrine was built facing west towards the [[Harima Sea]], but because boatmen passing by at sea did not worship there, it caused frequent curses, so it was changed to its current south-southwest orientation.]]{{complex}} '''[[Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji|Yamato Okunitama Shrine]]''' is [[Shinto shrine|a shrine]] located in Enamikamihata, {{ill|Minamiawaji|en|4=fr|lt=Minami Awaji City|12=draft}}, [[Hyogo Prefecture]]. It is a shrine listed in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] as a [[Myojin Taisha]] and is [[Ichinomiya|ninomiya]] or second ranked shrine in [[Awaji Province]], and [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|its former rank]] was [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|that of a prefectural shrine]]..{{Cite web|title=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|url=http://kuniumi-awaji.jp/|access-date=2024-04-07|website=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|language=en}} It is connected to the [[Yamato no Kuni no Miyatsuko|Yamato no Kuni no MIyatsuko]]. == deity == * Main deity: [[Yamato Okunitama|Yamato-Okunitama-no-kami]] * Associated deities: [[Ōkuninushi|Yasengai-no-Mikoto]], [[Toshigami|Oninoshi-no-Mikoto]], [[Susanoo|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]], [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]], [[Landlord deity|Earth God]] According to "A Fundamental Study on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Countries," the deities enshrined in the "Ippen Shonin E" and the Noh play "Awaji" are cited as [[Izanagi|Izanagi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Izanami|Izanami-no-Mikoto]], indicating that in the medieval period, the two deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 The book suggests that such an error occurred because Awaji is the land associated with the creation myth involving Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto, leading to this association by shrine families, as speculated in the "Shikinai-sha Report." It also states that the enshrinement returned to Yamato Okuninushi-no-Kami after the separation of Shinto and Buddhism in the Meiji period. The "Chuko Shujishi," dated August 1670 (Kanbun 10), was also written based on the theory that the deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.『中興趣意書』は、神道大系編纂会編 『神道大系 神社編41 紀伊・淡路国』 神道大系編纂会 1987th year 9月 に所収されている。 == history == The exact date of construction of this shrine is unknown. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, when the power of {{ill|Yamato kingship|lt=the Yamato Imperial Court|en|12=draft}} extended to Awaji, this shrine is believed to have {{ill|Bunrei|lt=enshrined|En|12=draft}} Yamato-no-Okunitama-jinja Shrine (present-day [[Ōyamato Shrine|Yamato Shrine]] ) in {{ill|Yamabe District, Nara|lt=Yamabe District|en|12=draft}}, [[Yamato Province]], in prayer for the stability of its rule. The book "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in the Medieval Provinces" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 introduces the theory that the shrine was established in the 5th century, in connection with the rule of the Yamato court. According to the entry for December 5th, 851 in the " {{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|en}} ," this shrine was designated an official shrine by imperial decree. Furthermore, the entry for January 27, 859 in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|12=draft}} records that the shrine's {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|en|12=draft}} was promoted from Junior Second Rank and Third Class to Junior First Rank . In the year 927 (Engi 5), according to the "Engishiki Jinmyocho," it was designated as a Shikinaisha, and a [[Myojin Taisha]]. Additionally, in the "Sozei" section of the "Engishiki," it received 800 bundles of festival rations (equivalent to 16 koku of rice) from the state. According to the "Engishiki," at that time, only three other shrines besides [[Dewa Province]]'s [[Gassan Shrine]], [[Mutsu Province]]'s [[Shiogama Jinja|Shiogama Shrine]], and [[Izu Province]]'s {{ill|Mishima-taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|12=draft}} were receiving festival rations directly from the state's regular taxes, indicating that this shrine received special treatment from the state. This shrine is known as the second shrine of Awaji Province, but according to "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Various Provinces in the [[Eiman|Middle]] Ages" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。, the first mention of this was in the "Order for Annual Taxes from the Shrines of Various Shrines" 平安遺文3358号 『神祇官諸社年貢注文』は 竹内理三 編 『平安遺文 古文書編 第7巻』 株式会社東京堂出版 1963rd year 10月 に所収されている。 dated [[1165|June 1165]] (the first year of the Eiman era), which stated, "The second shrine of Awaji Province (50 baskets of charcoal and 100 bundles of firewood)." The book also cites the Gokokuji documents 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, including [[Genkyū|the Awaji]] Kokushicho Sensho '''庁宣'''は、現地に赴任しなかった[[国司]]が、[[国衙]]の在庁官人にあてた命令のこと。 dated April [[1205|1205 (the 2nd year of the Genkyu era]] ), which states, “It was ordered to quickly gather information about the First and Second Palace Hokke and Sakura festivals, as well as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields and wilderness areas.” This suggests that the {{ill|10=ja|11=国衙|provincial government|12=draft}} was in charge of the festivals of this shrine, as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields were allocated by the provincial government for the holding of both the Hokke and Sakura festivals. The stone monument in front of the shrine explains how the festival became known to the public as the "Ninomiya Cherry Blossom Festival" because local people would worship the gods and admire the cherry blossoms. Later, the shrine came to be revered as the Ninomiya of Awaji Province, and both the imperial court and the military government became deeply revered. In the past, this Sakura-e festival was held on March 10th, but according to "The Gods of Japan - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, it was discontinued at some point. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" [1 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in [[Shōō (Kamakura period)|July]] [[1289]], the monk {{ill|Ippen|en}} Shonin visited the shrine, composed a poem, wrote it on a wooden tablet, and nailed it to the front of the main shrine building. It is said that this wooden tablet was still there when {{ill|Shōkai|fr|12=draft}}, the editor of "Ippen Hijiri-e," visited the temple after Ippen's death. The book also says that when Ippen Shonin heard that the shrine's deity was Izanami-no-Mikoto, he offered fervent prayers, and even built a hut in front of the shrine, performed dancing {{ill|nembutsu|en}}, and handed out pieces of paper with the words "Namu Amida Butsu" written on them. According to the "Awaji Province Temple and Mountain Memorial Services Order," one of the "Gokokuji Documents" 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, bugaku (traditional dance) performances were offered to the shrine by musicians from Kashu Hachiman (Kashu Hachiman, Minamiawaji City). According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, this took place during [[Muromachi period|the Muromachi period]] . During [[Edo period|the Edo period]], Awaji Province became a fief of the Tokushima Domain, and the {{ill|Hachisuka clan|en|12=draft}} also had deep faith in this shrine, donating two tan of land to the shrine in [[1702]] ( [[Genroku]] 15). Since then, it has been revered as a place of prayer for generations, and the shrine buildings have been renovated many times. In addition to rebuilding the main hall, other [[Bunsei|constructions]], such as the construction of [[Tenpō|other]] halls in [[1829]] and [[1843]], were carried out until the {{ill|abolition of the han system|en|4=fr|5=Abolition du système han|12=draft}} and the establishment of prefectures following [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]] . Due to {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|lt=the Shinto-Buddhist separation order|en|12=draft}} in [[1868]], the Kannon Hall of Yamato-ji Temple, the 12th temple on the Awaji Saigoku Pilgrimage, and the Yakushi Hall, the 2nd temple on the Awaji Forty-nine Yakushi Temples, which were located within the shrine grounds, were moved outside. In [[1873]], under the old shrine ranking system, it was ranked as [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], and [[1877|in 1877]], the main hall and other buildings were all newly built using county funds from believers throughout {{ill|Mihara District, Hyōgo|lt=Mihara County|en|12=draft}}. When the {{ill|10=ja|11=阪神・淡路大震災|Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake|12=draft}} occurred on January 17, [[1995]], the torii gate, which had been erected approximately 400 years ago, was damaged beyond repair, so in December [[1998|1998,]] parishioners from the five districts of Somori, Kamihata, Shimohata, Matsuda, and Yamadokoro worked together to erect the current torii gate. == Festivals == * February 11th: [[National Foundation Day (Japan|National Foundation Day]] * February 17th [[Kinensai|Prayer Festival]] * April 1st {{ill|Reisai|fr|lt=Annual Festival|12=draft}} * July 18th Summer Festival * November 12th [[Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niiname-sai Festival]] == Cultural Assets == === Hyogo Prefecture designated cultural property === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Yamato Company Seal **: According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, the seal is an old bronze seal that was excavated from the temple grounds during [[Hōei|the Hoei era]], measuring 5.5 cm square and engraved with the words "Yamato Shrine Seal." According to the book, it is said to date back to the early Heian period. == footnote == == References == * Edited by Takeuchi Rizo, Heian Ibun Komonsho Volume 7, Tokyodo Publishing Co., Ltd., October 1963 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Series Editing Committee, " National History Series Volume 3: [[Nihon kōki|Nihon Koki]], Shoku Nihon Koki, Nihon Montoku Tenno Jitsuroku " Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., August 1966 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Editing Committee, ed., National History Series, Volume 4 : The Chronicles of the Three Generations of Japan, Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., April 1966 * Edited by the Hyogo Prefecture History Editing Committee, "Hyogo Prefecture History: Historical Materials, Middle Ages 1," Hyogo Prefecture, November 1983 * Kenichi Tanigawa (ed.), "Japanese Gods -Shrines and Sacred Places- 3: Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" Hakusuisha Publishing Co., Ltd., August 1984 * Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee (ed.) Shinto Taikei Shrines Vol. 41 Kii and Awaji Province Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee September 1987 * "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces" edited by the Study Group on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces, Iwata Shoin Co., Ltd., February 2000 {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{afc comment|1=see [[every:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] for the history[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 02:26, 31 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Hyōgo Prefecture]] [[Category:Coordinates on Wikidata]] [[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[Category:Fuken-sha]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:Simple english wikipedia and everybodywiki]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq]] }} [[en:draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[fr:Yamato_Okunitama-jinja,_Minamiawaji]] [[en:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[sn:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[en:Draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[ja:大和大国魂神社]] [[fr:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama-jinja]]

According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in ancient times the shrine was built facing west towards the [[Harima Sea]], but because boatmen passing by at sea did not worship there, it caused frequent curses, so it was changed to its current south-southwest orientation.]]{{complex}} '''[[Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji|Yamato Okunitama Shrine]]''' is [[Shinto shrine|a shrine]] located in Enamikamihata, {{ill|Minamiawaji|en|4=fr|lt=Minami Awaji City|12=draft}}, [[Hyogo Prefecture]]. It is a shrine listed in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] as a [[Myojin Taisha]] and is [[Ichinomiya|ninomiya]] or second ranked shrine in [[Awaji Province]], and [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|its former rank]] was [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|that of a prefectural shrine]]..{{Cite web|title=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|url=http://kuniumi-awaji.jp/|access-date=2024-04-07|website=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|language=en}} It is connected to the [[Yamato no Kuni no Miyatsuko|Yamato no Kuni no MIyatsuko]]. == deity == * Main deity: [[Yamato Okunitama|Yamato-Okunitama-no-kami]] * Associated deities: [[Ōkuninushi|Yasengai-no-Mikoto]], [[Toshigami|Oninoshi-no-Mikoto]], [[Susanoo|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]], [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]], [[Landlord deity|Earth God]] According to "A Fundamental Study on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Countries," the deities enshrined in the "Ippen Shonin E" and the Noh play "Awaji" are cited as [[Izanagi|Izanagi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Izanami|Izanami-no-Mikoto]], indicating that in the medieval period, the two deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 The book suggests that such an error occurred because Awaji is the land associated with the creation myth involving Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto, leading to this association by shrine families, as speculated in the "Shikinai-sha Report." It also states that the enshrinement returned to Yamato Okuninushi-no-Kami after the separation of Shinto and Buddhism in the Meiji period. The "Chuko Shujishi," dated August 1670 (Kanbun 10), was also written based on the theory that the deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.『中興趣意書』は、神道大系編纂会編 『神道大系 神社編41 紀伊・淡路国』 神道大系編纂会 1987th year 9月 に所収されている。 == history == The exact date of construction of this shrine is unknown. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, when the power of {{ill|Yamato kingship|lt=the Yamato Imperial Court|en|12=draft}} extended to Awaji, this shrine is believed to have {{ill|Bunrei|lt=enshrined|En|12=draft}} Yamato-no-Okunitama-jinja Shrine (present-day [[Ōyamato Shrine|Yamato Shrine]] ) in {{ill|Yamabe District, Nara|lt=Yamabe District|en|12=draft}}, [[Yamato Province]], in prayer for the stability of its rule. The book "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in the Medieval Provinces" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 introduces the theory that the shrine was established in the 5th century, in connection with the rule of the Yamato court. According to the entry for December 5th, 851 in the " {{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|en}} ," this shrine was designated an official shrine by imperial decree. Furthermore, the entry for January 27, 859 in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|12=draft}} records that the shrine's {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|en|12=draft}} was promoted from Junior Second Rank and Third Class to Junior First Rank . In the year 927 (Engi 5), according to the "Engishiki Jinmyocho," it was designated as a Shikinaisha, and a [[Myojin Taisha]]. Additionally, in the "Sozei" section of the "Engishiki," it received 800 bundles of festival rations (equivalent to 16 koku of rice) from the state. According to the "Engishiki," at that time, only three other shrines besides [[Dewa Province]]'s [[Gassan Shrine]], [[Mutsu Province]]'s [[Shiogama Jinja|Shiogama Shrine]], and [[Izu Province]]'s {{ill|Mishima-taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|12=draft}} were receiving festival rations directly from the state's regular taxes, indicating that this shrine received special treatment from the state. This shrine is known as the second shrine of Awaji Province, but according to "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Various Provinces in the [[Eiman|Middle]] Ages" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。, the first mention of this was in the "Order for Annual Taxes from the Shrines of Various Shrines" 平安遺文3358号 『神祇官諸社年貢注文』は 竹内理三 編 『平安遺文 古文書編 第7巻』 株式会社東京堂出版 1963rd year 10月 に所収されている。 dated [[1165|June 1165]] (the first year of the Eiman era), which stated, "The second shrine of Awaji Province (50 baskets of charcoal and 100 bundles of firewood)." The book also cites the Gokokuji documents 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, including [[Genkyū|the Awaji]] Kokushicho Sensho '''庁宣'''は、現地に赴任しなかった[[国司]]が、[[国衙]]の在庁官人にあてた命令のこと。 dated April [[1205|1205 (the 2nd year of the Genkyu era]] ), which states, “It was ordered to quickly gather information about the First and Second Palace Hokke and Sakura festivals, as well as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields and wilderness areas.” This suggests that the {{ill|10=ja|11=国衙|provincial government|12=draft}} was in charge of the festivals of this shrine, as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields were allocated by the provincial government for the holding of both the Hokke and Sakura festivals. The stone monument in front of the shrine explains how the festival became known to the public as the "Ninomiya Cherry Blossom Festival" because local people would worship the gods and admire the cherry blossoms. Later, the shrine came to be revered as the Ninomiya of Awaji Province, and both the imperial court and the military government became deeply revered. In the past, this Sakura-e festival was held on March 10th, but according to "The Gods of Japan - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, it was discontinued at some point. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" [1 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in [[Shōō (Kamakura period)|July]] [[1289]], the monk {{ill|Ippen|en}} Shonin visited the shrine, composed a poem, wrote it on a wooden tablet, and nailed it to the front of the main shrine building. It is said that this wooden tablet was still there when {{ill|Shōkai|fr|12=draft}}, the editor of "Ippen Hijiri-e," visited the temple after Ippen's death. The book also says that when Ippen Shonin heard that the shrine's deity was Izanami-no-Mikoto, he offered fervent prayers, and even built a hut in front of the shrine, performed dancing {{ill|nembutsu|en}}, and handed out pieces of paper with the words "Namu Amida Butsu" written on them. According to the "Awaji Province Temple and Mountain Memorial Services Order," one of the "Gokokuji Documents" 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, bugaku (traditional dance) performances were offered to the shrine by musicians from Kashu Hachiman (Kashu Hachiman, Minamiawaji City). According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, this took place during [[Muromachi period|the Muromachi period]] . During [[Edo period|the Edo period]], Awaji Province became a fief of the Tokushima Domain, and the {{ill|Hachisuka clan|en|12=draft}} also had deep faith in this shrine, donating two tan of land to the shrine in [[1702]] ( [[Genroku]] 15). Since then, it has been revered as a place of prayer for generations, and the shrine buildings have been renovated many times. In addition to rebuilding the main hall, other [[Bunsei|constructions]], such as the construction of [[Tenpō|other]] halls in [[1829]] and [[1843]], were carried out until the {{ill|abolition of the han system|en|4=fr|5=Abolition du système han|12=draft}} and the establishment of prefectures following [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]] . Due to {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|lt=the Shinto-Buddhist separation order|en|12=draft}} in [[1868]], the Kannon Hall of Yamato-ji Temple, the 12th temple on the Awaji Saigoku Pilgrimage, and the Yakushi Hall, the 2nd temple on the Awaji Forty-nine Yakushi Temples, which were located within the shrine grounds, were moved outside. In [[1873]], under the old shrine ranking system, it was ranked as [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], and [[1877|in 1877]], the main hall and other buildings were all newly built using county funds from believers throughout {{ill|Mihara District, Hyōgo|lt=Mihara County|en|12=draft}}. When the {{ill|10=ja|11=阪神・淡路大震災|Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake|12=draft}} occurred on January 17, [[1995]], the torii gate, which had been erected approximately 400 years ago, was damaged beyond repair, so in December [[1998|1998,]] parishioners from the five districts of Somori, Kamihata, Shimohata, Matsuda, and Yamadokoro worked together to erect the current torii gate. == Festivals == * February 11th: [[National Foundation Day (Japan|National Foundation Day]] * February 17th [[Kinensai|Prayer Festival]] * April 1st {{ill|Reisai|fr|lt=Annual Festival|12=draft}} * July 18th Summer Festival * November 12th [[Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niiname-sai Festival]] == Cultural Assets == === Hyogo Prefecture designated cultural property === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Yamato Company Seal **: According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, the seal is an old bronze seal that was excavated from the temple grounds during [[Hōei|the Hoei era]], measuring 5.5 cm square and engraved with the words "Yamato Shrine Seal." According to the book, it is said to date back to the early Heian period. == footnote == == References == * Edited by Takeuchi Rizo, Heian Ibun Komonsho Volume 7, Tokyodo Publishing Co., Ltd., October 1963 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Series Editing Committee, " National History Series Volume 3: [[Nihon kōki|Nihon Koki]], Shoku Nihon Koki, Nihon Montoku Tenno Jitsuroku " Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., August 1966 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Editing Committee, ed., National History Series, Volume 4 : The Chronicles of the Three Generations of Japan, Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., April 1966 * Edited by the Hyogo Prefecture History Editing Committee, "Hyogo Prefecture History: Historical Materials, Middle Ages 1," Hyogo Prefecture, November 1983 * Kenichi Tanigawa (ed.), "Japanese Gods -Shrines and Sacred Places- 3: Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" Hakusuisha Publishing Co., Ltd., August 1984 * Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee (ed.) Shinto Taikei Shrines Vol. 41 Kii and Awaji Province Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee September 1987 * "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces" edited by the Study Group on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces, Iwata Shoin Co., Ltd., February 2000 {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{afc comment|1=see [[every:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] for the history[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 02:26, 31 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Hyōgo Prefecture]] [[Category:Coordinates on Wikidata]] [[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[Category:Fuken-sha]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:Simple english wikipedia and everybodywiki]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq]] }} [[en:draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[fr:Yamato_Okunitama-jinja,_Minamiawaji]] [[en:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[sn:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[en:Draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[ja:大和大国魂神社]] [[fr:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama-jinja]]

According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, this took place during [[Muromachi period|the Muromachi period]] . During [[Edo period|the Edo period]], Awaji Province became a fief of the Tokushima Domain, and the {{ill|Hachisuka clan|en|12=draft}} also had deep faith in this shrine, donating two tan of land to the shrine in [[1702]] ( [[Genroku]] 15). Since then, it has been revered as a place of prayer for generations, and the shrine buildings have been renovated many times. In addition to rebuilding the main hall, other [[Bunsei|constructions]], such as the construction of [[Tenpō|other]] halls in [[1829]] and [[1843]], were carried out until the {{ill|abolition of the han system|en|4=fr|5=Abolition du système han|12=draft}} and the establishment of prefectures following [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]] . Due to {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|lt=the Shinto-Buddhist separation order|en|12=draft}} in [[1868]], the Kannon Hall of Yamato-ji Temple, the 12th temple on the Awaji Saigoku Pilgrimage, and the Yakushi Hall, the 2nd temple on the Awaji Forty-nine Yakushi Temples, which were located within the shrine grounds, were moved outside. In [[1873]], under the old shrine ranking system, it was ranked as [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], and [[1877|in 1877]], the main hall and other buildings were all newly built using county funds from believers throughout {{ill|Mihara District, Hyōgo|lt=Mihara County|en|12=draft}}. When the {{ill|10=ja|11=阪神・淡路大震災|Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake|12=draft}} occurred on January 17, [[1995]], the torii gate, which had been erected approximately 400 years ago, was damaged beyond repair, so in December [[1998|1998,]] parishioners from the five districts of Somori, Kamihata, Shimohata, Matsuda, and Yamadokoro worked together to erect the current torii gate. == Festivals == * February 11th: [[National Foundation Day (Japan|National Foundation Day]] * February 17th [[Kinensai|Prayer Festival]] * April 1st {{ill|Reisai|fr|lt=Annual Festival|12=draft}} * July 18th Summer Festival * November 12th [[Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niiname-sai Festival]] == Cultural Assets == === Hyogo Prefecture designated cultural property === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Yamato Company Seal **: According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, the seal is an old bronze seal that was excavated from the temple grounds during [[Hōei|the Hoei era]], measuring 5.5 cm square and engraved with the words "Yamato Shrine Seal." According to the book, it is said to date back to the early Heian period. == footnote == == References == * Edited by Takeuchi Rizo, Heian Ibun Komonsho Volume 7, Tokyodo Publishing Co., Ltd., October 1963 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Series Editing Committee, " National History Series Volume 3: [[Nihon kōki|Nihon Koki]], Shoku Nihon Koki, Nihon Montoku Tenno Jitsuroku " Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., August 1966 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Editing Committee, ed., National History Series, Volume 4 : The Chronicles of the Three Generations of Japan, Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., April 1966 * Edited by the Hyogo Prefecture History Editing Committee, "Hyogo Prefecture History: Historical Materials, Middle Ages 1," Hyogo Prefecture, November 1983 * Kenichi Tanigawa (ed.), "Japanese Gods -Shrines and Sacred Places- 3: Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" Hakusuisha Publishing Co., Ltd., August 1984 * Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee (ed.) Shinto Taikei Shrines Vol. 41 Kii and Awaji Province Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee September 1987 * "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces" edited by the Study Group on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces, Iwata Shoin Co., Ltd., February 2000 {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{afc comment|1=see [[every:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] for the history[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 02:26, 31 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Hyōgo Prefecture]] [[Category:Coordinates on Wikidata]] [[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[Category:Fuken-sha]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[Category:Simple english wikipedia and everybodywiki]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq]] }} [[en:draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[fr:Yamato_Okunitama-jinja,_Minamiawaji]] [[en:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[sn:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[en:Draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[ja:大和大国魂神社]] [[fr:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama-jinja]]

According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in ancient times the shrine was built facing west towards the [[Harima Sea]], but because boatmen passing by at sea did not worship there, it caused frequent curses, so it was changed to its current south-southwest orientation.]]{{complex}} '''[[Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji|Yamato Okunitama Shrine]]''' is [[Shinto shrine|a shrine]] located in Enamikamihata, {{ill|Minamiawaji|en|4=fr|lt=Minami Awaji City|12=draft}}, [[Hyogo Prefecture]]. It is a shrine listed in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] as a [[Myojin Taisha]] and is [[Ichinomiya|ninomiya]] or second ranked shrine in [[Awaji Province]], and [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|its former rank]] was [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|that of a prefectural shrine]]..{{Cite web|title=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|url=http://kuniumi-awaji.jp/|access-date=2024-04-07|website=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|language=en}} It is connected to the [[Yamato no Kuni no Miyatsuko|Yamato no Kuni no MIyatsuko]]. == deity == * Main deity: [[Yamato Okunitama|Yamato-Okunitama-no-kami]] * Associated deities: [[Ōkuninushi|Yasengai-no-Mikoto]], [[Toshigami|Oninoshi-no-Mikoto]], [[Susanoo|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]], [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]], [[Landlord deity|Earth God]] According to "A Fundamental Study on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Countries," the deities enshrined in the "Ippen Shonin E" and the Noh play "Awaji" are cited as [[Izanagi|Izanagi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Izanami|Izanami-no-Mikoto]], indicating that in the medieval period, the two deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 The book suggests that such an error occurred because Awaji is the land associated with the creation myth involving Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto, leading to this association by shrine families, as speculated in the "Shikinai-sha Report." It also states that the enshrinement returned to Yamato Okuninushi-no-Kami after the separation of Shinto and Buddhism in the Meiji period. The "Chuko Shujishi," dated August 1670 (Kanbun 10), was also written based on the theory that the deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.『中興趣意書』は、神道大系編纂会編 『神道大系 神社編41 紀伊・淡路国』 神道大系編纂会 1987th year 9月 に所収されている。 == history == The exact date of construction of this shrine is unknown. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, when the power of {{ill|Yamato kingship|lt=the Yamato Imperial Court|en|12=draft}} extended to Awaji, this shrine is believed to have {{ill|Bunrei|lt=enshrined|En|12=draft}} Yamato-no-Okunitama-jinja Shrine (present-day [[Ōyamato Shrine|Yamato Shrine]] ) in {{ill|Yamabe District, Nara|lt=Yamabe District|en|12=draft}}, [[Yamato Province]], in prayer for the stability of its rule. The book "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in the Medieval Provinces" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 introduces the theory that the shrine was established in the 5th century, in connection with the rule of the Yamato court. According to the entry for December 5th, 851 in the " {{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|en}} ," this shrine was designated an official shrine by imperial decree. Furthermore, the entry for January 27, 859 in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|12=draft}} records that the shrine's {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|en|12=draft}} was promoted from Junior Second Rank and Third Class to Junior First Rank . In the year 927 (Engi 5), according to the "Engishiki Jinmyocho," it was designated as a Shikinaisha, and a [[Myojin Taisha]]. Additionally, in the "Sozei" section of the "Engishiki," it received 800 bundles of festival rations (equivalent to 16 koku of rice) from the state. According to the "Engishiki," at that time, only three other shrines besides [[Dewa Province]]'s [[Gassan Shrine]], [[Mutsu Province]]'s [[Shiogama Jinja|Shiogama Shrine]], and [[Izu Province]]'s {{ill|Mishima-taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|12=draft}} were receiving festival rations directly from the state's regular taxes, indicating that this shrine received special treatment from the state. This shrine is known as the second shrine of Awaji Province, but according to "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Various Provinces in the [[Eiman|Middle]] Ages" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。, the first mention of this was in the "Order for Annual Taxes from the Shrines of Various Shrines" 平安遺文3358号 『神祇官諸社年貢注文』は 竹内理三 編 『平安遺文 古文書編 第7巻』 株式会社東京堂出版 1963rd year 10月 に所収されている。 dated [[1165|June 1165]] (the first year of the Eiman era), which stated, "The second shrine of Awaji Province (50 baskets of charcoal and 100 bundles of firewood)." The book also cites the Gokokuji documents 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, including [[Genkyū|the Awaji]] Kokushicho Sensho '''庁宣'''は、現地に赴任しなかった[[国司]]が、[[国衙]]の在庁官人にあてた命令のこと。 dated April [[1205|1205 (the 2nd year of the Genkyu era]] ), which states, “It was ordered to quickly gather information about the First and Second Palace Hokke and Sakura festivals, as well as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields and wilderness areas.” This suggests that the {{ill|10=ja|11=国衙|provincial government|12=draft}} was in charge of the festivals of this shrine, as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields were allocated by the provincial government for the holding of both the Hokke and Sakura festivals. The stone monument in front of the shrine explains how the festival became known to the public as the "Ninomiya Cherry Blossom Festival" because local people would worship the gods and admire the cherry blossoms. Later, the shrine came to be revered as the Ninomiya of Awaji Province, and both the imperial court and the military government became deeply revered. In the past, this Sakura-e festival was held on March 10th, but according to "The Gods of Japan - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, it was discontinued at some point. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" [1 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in [[Shōō (Kamakura period)|July]] [[1289]], the monk {{ill|Ippen|en}} Shonin visited the shrine, composed a poem, wrote it on a wooden tablet, and nailed it to the front of the main shrine building. It is said that this wooden tablet was still there when {{ill|Shōkai|fr|12=draft}}, the editor of "Ippen Hijiri-e," visited the temple after Ippen's death. The book also says that when Ippen Shonin heard that the shrine's deity was Izanami-no-Mikoto, he offered fervent prayers, and even built a hut in front of the shrine, performed dancing {{ill|nembutsu|en}}, and handed out pieces of paper with the words "Namu Amida Butsu" written on them. According to the "Awaji Province Temple and Mountain Memorial Services Order," one of the "Gokokuji Documents" 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, bugaku (traditional dance) performances were offered to the shrine by musicians from Kashu Hachiman (Kashu Hachiman, Minamiawaji City). According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, this took place during [[Muromachi period|the Muromachi period]] . During [[Edo period|the Edo period]], Awaji Province became a fief of the Tokushima Domain, and the {{ill|Hachisuka clan|en|12=draft}} also had deep faith in this shrine, donating two tan of land to the shrine in [[1702]] ( [[Genroku]] 15). Since then, it has been revered as a place of prayer for generations, and the shrine buildings have been renovated many times. In addition to rebuilding the main hall, other [[Bunsei|constructions]], such as the construction of [[Tenpō|other]] halls in [[1829]] and [[1843]], were carried out until the {{ill|abolition of the han system|en|4=fr|5=Abolition du système han|12=draft}} and the establishment of prefectures following [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]] . Due to {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|lt=the Shinto-Buddhist separation order|en|12=draft}} in [[1868]], the Kannon Hall of Yamato-ji Temple, the 12th temple on the Awaji Saigoku Pilgrimage, and the Yakushi Hall, the 2nd temple on the Awaji Forty-nine Yakushi Temples, which were located within the shrine grounds, were moved outside. In [[1873]], under the old shrine ranking system, it was ranked as [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], and [[1877|in 1877]], the main hall and other buildings were all newly built using county funds from believers throughout {{ill|Mihara District, Hyōgo|lt=Mihara County|en|12=draft}}. When the {{ill|10=ja|11=阪神・淡路大震災|Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake|12=draft}} occurred on January 17, [[1995]], the torii gate, which had been erected approximately 400 years ago, was damaged beyond repair, so in December [[1998|1998,]] parishioners from the five districts of Somori, Kamihata, Shimohata, Matsuda, and Yamadokoro worked together to erect the current torii gate. == Festivals == * February 11th: [[National Foundation Day (Japan|National Foundation Day]] * February 17th [[Kinensai|Prayer Festival]] * April 1st {{ill|Reisai|fr|lt=Annual Festival|12=draft}} * July 18th Summer Festival * November 12th [[Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niiname-sai Festival]] == Cultural Assets == === Hyogo Prefecture designated cultural property === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Yamato Company Seal **: According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, the seal is an old bronze seal that was excavated from the temple grounds during [[Hōei|the Hoei era]], measuring 5.5 cm square and engraved with the words "Yamato Shrine Seal." According to the book, it is said to date back to the early Heian period. == footnote == == References == * Edited by Takeuchi Rizo, Heian Ibun Komonsho Volume 7, Tokyodo Publishing Co., Ltd., October 1963 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Series Editing Committee, " National History Series Volume 3: [[Nihon kōki|Nihon Koki]], Shoku Nihon Koki, Nihon Montoku Tenno Jitsuroku " Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., August 1966 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Editing Committee, ed., National History Series, Volume 4 : The Chronicles of the Three Generations of Japan, Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., April 1966 * Edited by the Hyogo Prefecture History Editing Committee, "Hyogo Prefecture History: Historical Materials, Middle Ages 1," Hyogo Prefecture, November 1983 * Kenichi Tanigawa (ed.), "Japanese Gods -Shrines and Sacred Places- 3: Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" Hakusuisha Publishing Co., Ltd., August 1984 * Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee (ed.) Shinto Taikei Shrines Vol. 41 Kii and Awaji Province Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee September 1987 * "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces" edited by the Study Group on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces, Iwata Shoin Co., Ltd., February 2000 {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{afc comment|1=see [[every:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] for the history[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 02:26, 31 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Hyōgo Prefecture]] [[Category:Coordinates on Wikidata]] [[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[Category:Fuken-sha]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[Category:Simple english wikipedia and everybodywiki]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:qq]] }} [[en:draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[fr:Yamato_Okunitama-jinja,_Minamiawaji]] [[en:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[sn:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[en:Draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[ja:大和大国魂神社]] [[fr:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama-jinja]]

According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in ancient times the shrine was built facing west towards the [[Harima Sea]], but because boatmen passing by at sea did not worship there, it caused frequent curses, so it was changed to its current south-southwest orientation.]]{{complex}} '''[[Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji|Yamato Okunitama Shrine]]''' is [[Shinto shrine|a shrine]] located in Enamikamihata, {{ill|Minamiawaji|en|4=fr|lt=Minami Awaji City|12=draft|12=draft}}, [[Hyogo Prefecture]]. It is a shrine listed in the [[Engishiki Jinmyocho]] as a [[Myojin Taisha]] and is [[Ichinomiya|ninomiya]] or second ranked shrine in [[Awaji Province]], and [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|its former rank]] was [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|that of a prefectural shrine]]..{{Cite web|title=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|url=http://kuniumi-awaji.jp/|access-date=2024-04-07|website=Awaji Island Japan Heritage {{!}} Ama who supported the ancient state|language=en}} It is connected to the [[Yamato no Kuni no Miyatsuko|Yamato no Kuni no MIyatsuko]]. == deity == * Main deity: [[Yamato Okunitama|Yamato-Okunitama-no-kami]] * Associated deities: [[Ōkuninushi|Yasengai-no-Mikoto]], [[Toshigami|Oninoshi-no-Mikoto]], [[Susanoo|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]], [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi-no-Mikoto]], [[Landlord deity|Earth God]] According to "A Fundamental Study on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Countries," the deities enshrined in the "Ippen Shonin E" and the Noh play "Awaji" are cited as [[Izanagi|Izanagi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Izanami|Izanami-no-Mikoto]], indicating that in the medieval period, the two deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 The book suggests that such an error occurred because Awaji is the land associated with the creation myth involving Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto, leading to this association by shrine families, as speculated in the "Shikinai-sha Report." It also states that the enshrinement returned to Yamato Okuninushi-no-Kami after the separation of Shinto and Buddhism in the Meiji period. The "Chuko Shujishi," dated August 1670 (Kanbun 10), was also written based on the theory that the deities enshrined were Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto.『中興趣意書』は、神道大系編纂会編 『神道大系 神社編41 紀伊・淡路国』 神道大系編纂会 1987th year 9月 に所収されている。 == history == The exact date of construction of this shrine is unknown. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, when the power of {{ill|Yamato kingship|lt=the Yamato Imperial Court|en|12=draft|12=draft}} extended to Awaji, this shrine is believed to have {{ill|Bunrei|lt=enshrined|En|12=draft|12=draft}} Yamato-no-Okunitama-jinja Shrine (present-day [[Ōyamato Shrine|Yamato Shrine]] ) in {{ill|Yamabe District, Nara|lt=Yamabe District|en|12=draft|12=draft}}, [[Yamato Province]], in prayer for the stability of its rule. The book "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in the Medieval Provinces" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。 introduces the theory that the shrine was established in the 5th century, in connection with the rule of the Yamato court. According to the entry for December 5th, 851 in the " {{ill|Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|en}} ," this shrine was designated an official shrine by imperial decree. Furthermore, the entry for January 27, 859 in the {{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|en|12=draft|12=draft}} records that the shrine's {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|lt=divine rank|en|12=draft|12=draft}} was promoted from Junior Second Rank and Third Class to Junior First Rank . In the year 927 (Engi 5), according to the "Engishiki Jinmyocho," it was designated as a Shikinaisha, and a [[Myojin Taisha]]. Additionally, in the "Sozei" section of the "Engishiki," it received 800 bundles of festival rations (equivalent to 16 koku of rice) from the state. According to the "Engishiki," at that time, only three other shrines besides [[Dewa Province]]'s [[Gassan Shrine]], [[Mutsu Province]]'s [[Shiogama Jinja|Shiogama Shrine]], and [[Izu Province]]'s {{ill|Mishima-taisha|en|Mishima Taisha|12=draft|12=draft}} were receiving festival rations directly from the state's regular taxes, indicating that this shrine received special treatment from the state. This shrine is known as the second shrine of Awaji Province, but according to "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Various Provinces in the [[Eiman|Middle]] Ages" 中世諸国一宮制研究会編 『中世諸国一宮制の基礎的研究』 ㈲岩田書院 2000th year 2月 より。, the first mention of this was in the "Order for Annual Taxes from the Shrines of Various Shrines" 平安遺文3358号 『神祇官諸社年貢注文』は 竹内理三 編 『平安遺文 古文書編 第7巻』 株式会社東京堂出版 1963rd year 10月 に所収されている。 dated [[1165|June 1165]] (the first year of the Eiman era), which stated, "The second shrine of Awaji Province (50 baskets of charcoal and 100 bundles of firewood)." The book also cites the Gokokuji documents 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, including [[Genkyū|the Awaji]] Kokushicho Sensho '''庁宣'''は、現地に赴任しなかった[[国司]]が、[[国衙]]の在庁官人にあてた命令のこと。 dated April [[1205|1205 (the 2nd year of the Genkyu era]] ), which states, “It was ordered to quickly gather information about the First and Second Palace Hokke and Sakura festivals, as well as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields and wilderness areas.” This suggests that the {{ill|10=ja|11=国衙|provincial government|12=draft|12=draft}} was in charge of the festivals of this shrine, as 10 cho of Bugaku rice fields were allocated by the provincial government for the holding of both the Hokke and Sakura festivals. The stone monument in front of the shrine explains how the festival became known to the public as the "Ninomiya Cherry Blossom Festival" because local people would worship the gods and admire the cherry blossoms. Later, the shrine came to be revered as the Ninomiya of Awaji Province, and both the imperial court and the military government became deeply revered. In the past, this Sakura-e festival was held on March 10th, but according to "The Gods of Japan - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, it was discontinued at some point. According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" [1 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, in [[Shōō (Kamakura period)|July]] [[1289]], the monk {{ill|Ippen|en}} Shonin visited the shrine, composed a poem, wrote it on a wooden tablet, and nailed it to the front of the main shrine building. It is said that this wooden tablet was still there when {{ill|Shōkai|fr|12=draft|12=draft}}, the editor of "Ippen Hijiri-e," visited the temple after Ippen's death. The book also says that when Ippen Shonin heard that the shrine's deity was Izanami-no-Mikoto, he offered fervent prayers, and even built a hut in front of the shrine, performed dancing {{ill|nembutsu|en}}, and handed out pieces of paper with the words "Namu Amida Butsu" written on them. According to the "Awaji Province Temple and Mountain Memorial Services Order," one of the "Gokokuji Documents" 「護国寺文書」は、兵庫県史編集専門委員会 編 『兵庫県史 史料編 中世1』 兵庫県 1983rd year 11月 に所収されている。, bugaku (traditional dance) performances were offered to the shrine by musicians from Kashu Hachiman (Kashu Hachiman, Minamiawaji City). According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3 Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, and Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, this took place during [[Muromachi period|the Muromachi period]] . During [[Edo period|the Edo period]], Awaji Province became a fief of the Tokushima Domain, and the {{ill|Hachisuka clan|en|12=draft|12=draft}} also had deep faith in this shrine, donating two tan of land to the shrine in [[1702]] ( [[Genroku]] 15). Since then, it has been revered as a place of prayer for generations, and the shrine buildings have been renovated many times. In addition to rebuilding the main hall, other [[Bunsei|constructions]], such as the construction of [[Tenpō|other]] halls in [[1829]] and [[1843]], were carried out until the {{ill|abolition of the han system|en|4=fr|5=Abolition du système han|12=draft|12=draft}} and the establishment of prefectures following [[Meiji Restoration|the Meiji Restoration]] . Due to {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|lt=the Shinto-Buddhist separation order|en|12=draft|12=draft}} in [[1868]], the Kannon Hall of Yamato-ji Temple, the 12th temple on the Awaji Saigoku Pilgrimage, and the Yakushi Hall, the 2nd temple on the Awaji Forty-nine Yakushi Temples, which were located within the shrine grounds, were moved outside. In [[1873]], under the old shrine ranking system, it was ranked as [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|a prefectural shrine]], and [[1877|in 1877]], the main hall and other buildings were all newly built using county funds from believers throughout {{ill|Mihara District, Hyōgo|lt=Mihara County|en|12=draft|12=draft}}. When the {{ill|10=ja|11=阪神・淡路大震災|Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake|12=draft|12=draft}} occurred on January 17, [[1995]], the torii gate, which had been erected approximately 400 years ago, was damaged beyond repair, so in December [[1998|1998,]] parishioners from the five districts of Somori, Kamihata, Shimohata, Matsuda, and Yamadokoro worked together to erect the current torii gate. == Festivals == * February 11th: [[National Foundation Day (Japan|National Foundation Day]] * February 17th [[Kinensai|Prayer Festival]] * April 1st {{ill|Reisai|fr|lt=Annual Festival|12=draft|12=draft}} * July 18th Summer Festival * November 12th [[Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niiname-sai Festival]] == Cultural Assets == === Hyogo Prefecture designated cultural property === * Important Cultural Property (Tangible Cultural Property) ** Yamato Company Seal **: According to "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 3, Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" 谷川健一 編 『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 3 摂津・河内・和泉・淡路』 株式会社白水社 1984th year 8月 より。, the seal is an old bronze seal that was excavated from the temple grounds during [[Hōei|the Hoei era]], measuring 5.5 cm square and engraved with the words "Yamato Shrine Seal." According to the book, it is said to date back to the early Heian period. == footnote == == References == * Edited by Takeuchi Rizo, Heian Ibun Komonsho Volume 7, Tokyodo Publishing Co., Ltd., October 1963 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Series Editing Committee, " National History Series Volume 3: [[Nihon kōki|Nihon Koki]], Shoku Nihon Koki, Nihon Montoku Tenno Jitsuroku " Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., August 1966 * Katsumi Kuroita, National History Editing Committee, ed., National History Series, Volume 4 : The Chronicles of the Three Generations of Japan, Yoshikawa Kobunkan Co., Ltd., April 1966 * Edited by the Hyogo Prefecture History Editing Committee, "Hyogo Prefecture History: Historical Materials, Middle Ages 1," Hyogo Prefecture, November 1983 * Kenichi Tanigawa (ed.), "Japanese Gods -Shrines and Sacred Places- 3: Settsu, Kawachi, Izumi, Awaji" Hakusuisha Publishing Co., Ltd., August 1984 * Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee (ed.) Shinto Taikei Shrines Vol. 41 Kii and Awaji Province Shinto Taikei Editorial Committee September 1987 * "Basic Research on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces" edited by the Study Group on the Ichinomiya System in Medieval Provinces, Iwata Shoin Co., Ltd., February 2000 {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} {{citation needed|Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji}} [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] [[simple:user:immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[simple:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama Shrine]] {{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Hyōgo Prefecture]] [[Category:Coordinates on Wikidata]] [[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Ninomiya]] [[Category:Fuken-sha]] [[Category:Completion tier 2]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[Category:Pages from Simple English Wikipedia]] [[Category:Simple english wikipedia and everybodywiki]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:qq]] }} [[en:draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[fr:Yamato_Okunitama-jinja,_Minamiawaji]] [[en:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[sn:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[en:Draft:Yamato Okunitama Shrine, Minamiawaji]] [[ja:大和大国魂神社]] [[fr:User:Immanuelle/Yamato Okunitama-jinja]]
